The source appears to be a video by Andrei Jikh discussing a hypothetical or projected global oil shock related to disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz. I found references to the video and reports repeating some of the same talking points.  

What I could partially verify

* The video did contain the claim that Australia was facing a fuel-supply crunch around April 19–20 and that emergency measures were being discussed.  
* Reports from that period discussed disruptions in oil shipments, concerns over the Strait of Hormuz, fuel tax reductions, reserve releases, and replacement shipments being sourced from elsewhere.  

Claims I could NOT verify from reliable sources

I did not find credible evidence supporting:

* Indonesia or Vietnam ordering broad work-from-home measures to conserve fuel.
* Thailand’s fishing industry shutting down because marine fuel rose 250%.
* Japan slowing ferry services because of fuel shortages.
* India halting LPG supplies for commercial users nationwide.
* 20% of Mumbai hotels and restaurants closing because of fuel shortages.
* Africa-wide fuel deliveries stopping April 10.
* Ethiopia, Zimbabwe, or South Sudan diluting gasoline with chemicals as official policy.
* Europe having deliveries stop April 10.

Those claims may have come from the video narrative, secondary social-media reposts, or localized reports, but I could not confirm them from authoritative sources.

The Australia fuel-security concern was a real discussion point.

looks substantially less supported. Several of the most dramatic claims either cannot be verified or appear exaggerated when compared with available reporting.

It has nothing to do with confidence. It's just a function of how many dollars are being deposited in foreign central banks, vs how many are being withdrawn. Foreign companies get paid in dollars from US buyers, and they have to pay in dollars for their components they source abroad, and if there's a surplus that's a net deposit in their central bank. When foreign central banks have excess dollars, they buy treasury bonds with them. When foreign central banks have to RAISE dollars, they sell those bonds.

For example, let's say you buy a Sony TV at Walmart. Those dollars get exported to Japan. MOST of them are deposited in the bank and exchanged for Yen, which Sony uses to pay their employees, domestic operating expenses, etc. SOME of those dollars will got to Taiwan, China and South Korea for chips and batteries and PCBs. Usually, companies like Sony are net depositors of dollars. But since the US economy hasn't been doing well due to decreasing real wages, the dollars we're exporting is less than the dollars that are needed to satisfy debts in the Eurodollar market. I.e. Sony has a revolving line of credit with their suppliers, so to pay their outstanding invoices, they now have to become net withdrawers of dollars. Meaning the central bank has to sell the bonds to raise those dollars.

NOBODY in the financial system doubts the US government's ability to repay. NOBODY actually WANTS to sell treasuries for any reason. They simply have no choice.

I.e. everyone who could take on debt was already saturated, and our population wasn't growing fast enough to create enough new debtors to originate the loans to create the money to service the previous generation of debtors. The reality is more nuanced than the video’s alarming framing suggests. Here’s what’s actually happening:

Is it true?

It’s partly true but significantly overstated. There’s a frequently repeated myth on social media that foreigners are selling US Treasury bonds in large quantities, often citing China, Japan, and Saudi Arabia. The reality is that foreign ownership of US Treasury debt has actually been increasing steadily — growing at about 10%, above the pace of the prior decade. ￼

That said, there are real shifts happening. Japan, the largest foreign holder with about $1 trillion in Treasuries, may start pulling back — because the Bank of Japan has been hiking rates and Japanese bond yields are now looking more attractive domestically for the first time since the 1990s. ￼ And China has reportedly been advising its banks to hold off on buying more Treasuries, and in some cases to trim holdings — partly to avoid losses in a volatile market. ￼

Could this cause a financial crisis?

It’s a real risk to watch, but not an imminent collapse scenario. A few key points:

	•	Selling large amounts of Treasuries would likely cause significant losses for the sellers themselves due to the market impact on their remaining holdings — so it’s self-limiting. ￼
	•	Treasuries remain in permanent demand as the world’s reserve currency collateral, used in financial transactions globally. ￼
	•	The bigger concern is structural: US public debt has climbed to a record $37.64 trillion, and annual interest payments have now surpassed $1 trillion. ￼

The scenario that worries economists most isn’t a sudden mass sell-off, but a slow erosion of foreign appetite that forces the US to offer higher yields to attract buyers — making the debt burden even more expensive. Worth keeping an eye on, but the “everything is breaking” framing is typical YouTube alarm-bait.

I’m no expert but I think he’s leaving out an important distinction which is that there’s a Primary Bond Market when the govt sells bonds to the Private Banks in their country. and a Secondary Bond Market where the Private Banks sell the bonds they hold to anyone who wants to buy them.  I think what he’s talking about here is the Secondary Bond Market.  As I understand it (and I may be wrong!) the government has no direct role in the Secondary Bond Market.  The govt issues a 10yr bond to one of the private banks, and in 10yrs the govt pays that bond out to whomever is holding it at that time.  As long as the govt has used the money from the Primary Bond Sale to do productive things in the country, then there’s no in principle issue.  however they did kinda mess-up this system when they introduced payment of interest on a regular basis, rather than making bond holders wait for the bond to mature.  That stuffs up the government’s cash flow (I think).  But Andrei’s insistence on saying “debt” when he means “bond” is a bit inflammatory as it encourages the idea that govt debt is bad the same way household debt is bad, which of course is untrue. the reason we have these two different words for these two different things is to help hold that distinction in the mind and blurring things by saying “debt” when you mean “govt bond” is misleading.  At least that’s my understanding.
